Voat Historians - What was the Ancient Greek's idea of democracy?

I'm more of an ancient Roman history buff but my Greek history is pretty good.

Basically Aristotle said that all systems of government are neutral. So in the case of democracy in the modern sense of the word it is neither good or bad it is just an organizational system. He did however create words for the good and bad versions. Democracy was interestingly enough the bad version or rule by the people; it literally translates to "mob rule". The good version he referred to as polity, "rule by the people". No one can say for sure, but I would imagine that in ancient Greece the idea of having everyone involved in government sounded like a terrible idea, with many people uneducated and trying to organize so many might have seemed so impractical it was nearly impossible. As it relates to the modern day democracy is just a system, and it can really only work with an engaged and well informed populace.

I think taking a position on conspiracy one way or the other, as a matter of fact, is silly. It should all be viewed probabilistically. People taking a definitive stance one way or the other leads to ignorance and confirmation bias. Take the moon landing for instance. A favorite argument people on the 'doubt side' like to hit on here is the Van Allen Belt. But I think they mostly don't really understand their own argument there and rather chose it after deciding the landing didn't happen and looking for "proof" to support their semi arbitrary position. It sounds good, so they repeat it.

Pop quiz there. Would lead shielding on the ship have been a smart idea? I suspect nearly all Van Allen types would say yes because it confirms simple biases: 'We couldn't get through those belts because of high radiation. At the radiologist lead stops radiation so to get through the Van Allen Belts we'd need a craft made of lead which we obviously didn't have.' In reality that would be an enormous and potentially fatal mistake. Beta particles + lead = braking/bremsstrahlung radiation = astronauts getting pounded with high intensity x-ray radiation. Incidentally the correct way to shield against the most prevalent alpha/beta particles in the belt is with light materials such as aluminum and simply minimizing the amount of time in it - exactly what NASA did.

That's just one example, but the point is that you can find a mountain of evidence to support or refute just about any position on anything. So by simply deciding one side is right (or wrong) you tend to become prejudiced and ill informed. Believing in things you have no definitive and objective knowledge of is foolish. At the same time completely disregarding things for which there is at least some clear and objective evidence, even if it goes against how you would like to believe, is equally foolish.
